paragraphs: One of the proofs that God (mighty and exalted) does not resemble things, and that nothing resembles Him in any respect at all, is that the resemblance of things to one another is only of two kinds: Mode 1: Substance-resemblance — things resemble each other in genus: as blackness resembles blackness, whiteness resembles whiteness; as movement resembles movement when they are in one direction; as two voices resemble one another when they are of one mode (of pitch, timbre, etc.). Mode 2: Accident-resemblance — things resemble each other in visible aspect and touch via the conditions (hayʾāt) that inhere in them: composition, separation, rest, motion, color, etc. — as a white thing resembles a white thing in appearance, as a square resembles a square, as a soft thing resembles a soft thing in touch. Now, God cannot resemble things in substance — for He is, in His very essence (nafsihi), different from every genus; were He of a genus, He would be classified into one of the existing classes, but He is not — He is the difference from every class by His own essence. […] He has no genus by which to ground a substance-resemblance.

[...] He cannot bear accidents, and cannot be in any of the places — for He is self-sufficient in His own essence, requiring nothing of the things. He existed eternally before them, requiring nothing of them. Since there is no third mode of resemblance beyond the two we have specified — and both modes are impossible of God — it is correct that God has no likeness and no equal of any sort.

If someone objects: do you not say that God is "an agent in the true sense" and "just"? And do you not similarly call others "agents" and "just"? Have you not thereby likened God to others? Reply: acts do not produce resemblance. We have said that resemblance arises only through the inherence (ḥulūl) of certain conditions in bodies — colors, shapes, etc. Acts, when they proceed from an agent, do not require the agent to resemble anyone else in carrying them out; what produces resemblance is the inherence-of-condition. Since God's acts do not inhere in Him, His being "agent" or "knower" or "just" does not produce resemblance with anyone, even though others are also called by these designations. If someone says: do not "saying God moves" and "saying a body moves" license the inference that "God resembles bodies in motion"? Reply: yes. So we deny that He moves. So why do you not deny that the term "agent" creates a resemblance to created agents? Reply: because "God moves" licenses the inherence-of-motion-in-God; "God acts" does not license inherence-of-action-in-God — His acts proceed from Him without inhering in Him. ---
